items.title: QDiff: Differential Testing of Quantum Software Stacks
items.matched: OpenQASM 3: A Broader and Deeper Quantum Assembly Language
items.result: Differential testing framework finds 6 instability sources across Qiskit, Cirq, and Pyquil (4 crash bugs, 2 root causes explaining 25 of 29 hardware divergences) while static circuit filtering reduces backend runs by 66%.
items.question: How to differentially test quantum software stacks across compilers, simulators, and hardware despite probabilistic outputs and severe execution costs?
items.limits: Evaluated on at most 5 qubits without quantum error correction; total fuzzing run time capped at seven days.
items.tools: QDiff · semantics-preserving source transformation · Kolmogorov-Smirnov test · cross entropy · L1 norm closeness testing
items.caption: Equivalent circuits and resulting measurement outcome probability distributions on ibmq_yorktown, showing distribution divergence caused by 18 idle moments on qubit 4.
items.abstract: Over the past few years, several quantum software stacks (QSS) have been developed in response to rapid hardware advances in quantum computing. A QSS includes a quantum programming language, an optimizing compiler that translates a quantum algorithm written in a high-level language into quantum gate instructions, a quantum simulator that emulates these instructions on a classical device, and a software controller that sends analog signals to a very expensive quantum hardware based on quantum circuits. In comparison to traditional compilers and architecture simulators, QSSes are difficult to tests due to the probabilistic nature of results, the lack of clear hardware specifications, and quantum programming complexity. This work devises a novel differential testing approach for QSSes, named QDIFF with three major innovations: (1) We generate input programs to be tested via semantics-preserving, source to source transformation to explore program variants. (2) We speed up differential testing by filtering out quantum circuits that are not worthwhile to execute on quantum hardware by analyzing static characteristics such as a circuit depth, 2 qubit gate operations, gate error rates, and T1 relaxation time. (3) We design an extensible equivalence checking mechanism via distribution comparison functions such as Kolmogorov Smirnov test and cross entropy

items.title: Machine learning quantum data to accelerate quantum Monte Carlo
items.result: Machine-learning surrogates compress quantum randomized-measurement data to bypass classical shadow postprocessing, enabling chemically accurate quantum-classical QMC on up to 40 qubits with 190-fold to 4,100-fold speedups.
items.question: How can the computational bottleneck of repeatedly reconstructing quantum trial-state overlaps from classical shadows during quantum Monte Carlo propagation be overcome?
items.prior: Hardware demonstrations of quantum-classical QMC were limited to 16 qubits and required over 13,000 GPU hours for a single calculation; 40-qubit postprocessing was estimated to take millions of CPU hours.
items.limits: Requires training determinants N_train ≪N_w N_τ; training stopped via experimental noise floor F to avoid overfitting finite measurement noise.
items.tools: Google Willow processor · auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) · Clifford matchgate classical shadows · neural quantum states (NQS) · nonorthogonal configuration interaction (NOCI)
items.caption: Energy error relative to infinite-shot reference versus qubit count (8 to 40 qubits) for hydrogen chains (b), and total classical CPU/GPU cost for brute-force shadow processing versus ML surrogate showing 190- to 4,100-fold speedups (c).
items.abstract: Simulating strongly correlated electrons in molecules and materials remains a central goal for quantum computing. A promising strategy uses quantum processors to prepare trial wavefunctions that guide classical quantum Monte Carlo (QMC). However, the enormous computational cost of repeatedly processing quantum measurements has severely limited the practical scalability of this approach. Here, we overcome this bottleneck by compressing quantum measurement data into machine-learning models that efficiently provide the wavefunction overlaps needed by QMC. This accelerates quantum-classical QMC by orders of magnitude, enabling chemically accurate simulations on up to 40 qubits, more than doubling the scale of previous hardware demonstrations with comparable accuracy. We demonstrate our approach on hydrogen chains and strongly correlated iron-sulfur clusters using measurements from Google's Willow processor. By enabling efficient reuse of quantum-state information on the classical coprocessor, our framework addresses a fundamental bottleneck in hybrid quantum algorithms that will persist even into the fault-tolerant era.

items.abstract: In this work, we focus on addressing challenges related to modelling the integration of conventional high-performance computing (HPC) and quantum computing (QC). We introduce the Quantum Assembly Compiler (QASC) for OpenQASM3.0 files. The compiler produces an executable that leverages the high-performance simulator QuEST to simulate quantum programs. Additionally, we introduce a performance modelling tool, QACC-perf, which can estimate the cost of integrating QC in classical HPC workflows, as well as the execution time of the quantum circuits. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of these tools in the context of multiscale quantum chemistry workflows using the ChemShell computational chemistry environment.

items.result: Introduced differentiable-digital-twin software framework `qruise-toolset` for atomic qubits, simulating single-qubit randomized benchmarking with error per Clifford of 1.11(30)×10⁻³ and achieving quantum volume of 2⁴=16 with 83.1% mean heavy-output probability.

items.limits: Demonstrated primarily in numerical simulation; subject to exponential resource scaling for full state and process tomography.

items.caption: Heavy-output probability per circuit for 200 random four-qubit square circuits of depth 4. The cumulative mean (solid line) stays at 83.1%, exceeding the 2/3 pass threshold (dashed line) to demonstrate a quantum volume of 16.
items.abstract: Quantum technologies based on individually controlled atoms are among the most promising platforms for scalable quantum computing, owing to their favorable coherence properties and controllability. Nonetheless, achieving reliable and high-fidelity gate operations remains challenging due to the sensitivity of these systems to noise and hardware imperfections. In this work, we introduce a comprehensive software toolset designed to model atomic quantum systems with high precision and simulate qubit gate dynamics. By integrating quantum optimal control and benchmarking techniques with automatic differentiation for efficient and accurate gradient-based optimization, the toolset enables significant improvements in gate performance. We demonstrate its capabilities through detailed case studies involving both neutral atoms and trapped ions, highlighting its effectiveness in enhancing quantum gate fidelities, and providing valuable insights for experimental implementation.

items.title: Trajectory-Dependent Decoherence and Leakage During Shuttling of Multi-Spin Qubits
items.authors: Yu-Ning Zhang, Aleksandr S. Mokeev, Maximilian Rimbach-Russ, David P. DiVincenzo, Viatcheslav V. Dobrovitski
items.matched: Quantum error correction with silicon spin qubits
items.result: Parallel shuttling minimizes decoherence and leakage at short shuttling distances, whereas sequential shuttling outperforms it over long distances across 2-, 3-, and 4-spin encodings; multi-spin fidelity loss and leakage decompose analytically into sums of at most seven pairwise spin error parameters ε_jk^P.
items.question: How do spatial and temporal correlations in magnetic noise affect dephasing and leakage during the shuttling of multi-spin logical qubits across different trajectories?
items.limits: Pure dephasing via rotating-frame secular Hamiltonian (neglecting x,y noise and spin relaxation). Neglects inter-spin exchange interaction during shuttling. Assumes stationary, isotropic Gaussian noise field.
items.tools: Gaussian random field model of spatio-temporal 1/f noise · mixed-unitary dephasing quantum channel · pairwise dephasing factor expansion · Pauli transfer matrix analysis
items.caption: Average fidelity loss 1-F_XO of a 3-spin exchange-only qubit versus dimensionless shuttling length λ for sequential, parallel, and triangular protocols across channel separations δ= 0.3, 0.6, 0.8. Parallel shuttling yields lower error at short range, whereas sequential shuttling wins at long range.
items.abstract: Logical qubits encoded in collective states of multiple spins are promising building blocks for large-scale semiconductor quantum processors. As novel fault-tolerant architectures increasingly rely on qubit shuttling, understanding decoherence of the shuttled multi-spin qubits becomes crucial. We analyze fidelity and leakage of the logical qubits dephased by the spatio-temporally correlated 1/f noise, considering two-, three-, and four-spin encodings. We study different shuttling protocols and establish that for all encodings generally, parallel shuttling provides the best protection against decoherence at short distances, whereas sequential shuttling outperforms others for long-range transport (although the exact boundaries depend on the specific device parameters). We explain this common behavior in terms of the dephasing factors of pairs of the shuttled spins; we provide explicit expressions for fidelities and leakage, thus enabling experimentalists to predict performance of the multi-spin qubits from only several independently measured pairwise dephasing factors. Our results establish a connection between shuttling trajectories, noise correlations, and qubit decoherence, and provide guidance for achieving noise-resilient shuttling in scalable semiconductor quantum processors.

items.title: Enhancing valley splitting in Si/SiGe Wiggle Well quantum dots through integrated stressor-gate architectures
items.matched: Colloquium : Advances in automation of quantum dot devices control
items.result: Compressively stressed surface TiN thin films induce shear strains exceeding 0.1% in underlying Si/SiGe quantum wells even when routed across gate stacks, yielding deterministic valley splittings above 100 μeV in long-period Wiggle Wells.
items.question: Can surface-deposited thin-film stressors generate and maintain the shear strain required for deterministic valley splitting in Si/SiGe Wiggle Well quantum dots when integrated with realistic gate stacks?
items.prior: Conventional gate electrodes generate shear strains of ~0.01% to ~0.025%, 4-10 times too small for strain-assisted Wiggle Wells.
items.limits: Numerical continuum elastic simulation rather than experimental fabrication; assumes residual stress is thickness-independent; high-strain region is narrow, limiting scalability beyond 1D to narrow multi-row quantum dot arrays.
items.tools: finite-element modeling (COMSOL Multiphysics) · TiN thin-film stressors · Si/SiGe Wiggle Well heterostructures
items.caption: Linecuts of shear strain across dot and charge-sensor channels in a realistic quad-dot device layout, showing induced ε_xy sustained above 0.1% across multiple dots.
items.abstract: Engineering large and reproducible valley splittings is essential for the scalable operation of silicon spin qubits. In Si/SiGe quantum dot devices, valley splitting arises predominantly from atomic-scale disorder and is therefore inherently random, motivating approaches that introduce a large deterministic contribution. Strain-assisted Wiggle Wells provide a route to deterministic valley splitting by combining an oscillatory Ge concentration in the Si well with shear strain; however, generating the required strain in a manner compatible with large-scale architectures remains a challenge. Here, we propose patterned stressed thin films as a scalable approach for generating shear strain in the quantum well of Si/SiGe quantum dot devices. Finite-element simulations show that compressively stressed TiN films can generate shear strains exceeding 0.1% at the quantum well, sufficient for deterministic valley splittings of hundreds of μeV in strain-assisted Wiggle Wells. We show that this strain can extend across multiple quantum dots and is maintained in realistic gate geometries, providing a fabrication-compatible approach for scaling deterministic valley splitting to quantum dot arrays.

items.title: Impact of multi-dot configurations on electron temperature and double quantum dot latching in gate-controlled qubit devices
items.matched: Colloquium : Advances in automation of quantum dot devices control
items.result: Using a biased single-electron transistor concurrently as charge sensor and reservoir heats the reservoir electron temperature to 229 mK at 50 µV bias and 799 mK at 250 µV, compared to 133 mK and 152 mK for an unbiased extended reservoir.
items.question: How does using a single-electron transistor simultaneously as a charge sensor and electron reservoir impact the probed electron temperature, spectroscopy, and double quantum dot latching behavior in spin qubit architectures?
items.prior: Extended reservoir baseline was 133 mK at 50 µV SET bias and 152 mK at 250 µV SET bias in the same device.
items.limits: Measured on two devices; dilution refrigerator base temperature < 10 mK; latching observability depends on integration time per point being shorter than the direct tunneling time (20 ms).
items.tools: Si/SiGe heterostructure quantum dots · Single-electron transistor (SET) charge sensing · Pulsed gate spectroscopy (PGS) · Dilution refrigerator base temperature below 10 mK
items.caption: Fermi fit broadening of the 0-1 transition plotted against mixing plate temperature for 50 µV, 150 µV, and 250 µV SET bias. It compares loading from an extended reservoir with loading from a dual-role reservoir-sensor SET, showing higher electron temperatures in the latter.
items.abstract: Many currently envisaged scalable architectures for Si/SiGe spin qubit devices utilize gate-controlled multi-dot configurations characterized by their peculiar Coulomb blockade physics. One example is the concurrent use of a single electron transistor (SET) as a charge sensor and as a reservoir for adjacent qubit quantum dots (QD). We find that the SET energy spectrum impacts pulsed gate spectroscopy of the QD when the SET simultaneously acts as the reservoir and the sensor. Then, using the qubit QD as a probe, we quantify how strongly the electron temperature of the SET depends on the applied bias. It surpasses a reference experiment by 100 mK even at 50 μV bias. Our results provide a strong incentive for choosing spin qubit initialization schemes which do not rely on coupling to the reservoir in such devices. Switching to a double quantum dot connected to a single reservoir, a frequent configuration for qubit readout, we finally demonstrate the tunability of the characteristic latching behavior by systematically mapping it in the few-electron stability diagram.

items.title: A Compiler for Fault Tolerant Quantum Computing
items.authors: Narasinga Rao Miniskar, Elaine Wong, Seyong Lee, Vicente Leyton-Ortega, Jeffrey S. Vetter, Travis S. Humble
items.matched: Noise-Adaptive Compiler Mappings for Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum Computers
items.result: FTQC provides an MLIR dialect with an ECC-aware type system; on the 20-qubit Pathfinder device, decoding lowered logical readout error by a factor of 3.3.
items.question: How can a quantum compiler preserve error-correcting code information and resource constraints while lowering logical circuits to physical backends?
items.limits: Logical error estimates use leading-order model; distillation tracks peak qubits rather than space-time volume; non-Clifford gates replaced with Clifford stand-ins in Stim; no threshold scaling shown.
items.tools: MLIR and ODS · OpenQASM 3.0 · QIR · Stim and PyMatching · 20-qubit Pathfinder (ORNL)
items.caption: In-pipeline compile time (parse plus passes) as a function of logical qubit count n across six benchmark circuit families. Near-linear families execute in under 6 ms at n=100, while QFT scales quadratically to 100 ms at n=51.
items.abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) needs compiler intermediate representations (IRs) that preserve error-correcting-code choices, syndrome information, and non-Clifford resource requirements through analysis, simulation, and hardware lowering. We report practical experience building FTQC, an open-source Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect that makes logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames typed static single assignment (SSA) values. Its error-correction-aware type system, two-level lowering design, and IR-resident resource analysis provide one inspectable pipeline to Open Quantum Assembly Language~3 (OpenQASM~3), the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR), Stim, and IQM hardware. Case studies across three code families show that typed metadata makes code-specific decisions verifiable and retargetable: on the 20-qubit Pathfinder at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3 times. They also expose hidden architectural costs: for a three-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT-3), a magic-state factory requires five times the peak qubits of the encoded circuit. These experiences demonstrate a practical foundation for developing and evaluating fault-tolerant compiler transformations across software and hardware targets.

items.title: Unified architecture for arbitrary two-qubit gates with neutral atoms
items.matched: Qiskit pulse: programming quantum computers through the cloud with pulses
items.result: Unified Rydberg-atom architecture realizes arbitrary two-qubit gates natively from an XXZ interaction by tuning the anisotropy J_z/J ∈[-1, 0] via an RF-dressed Förster resonance and shaping global microwave pulses.
items.question: Can neutral-atom quantum processors implement the full set of two-qubit gates natively rather than decomposing unitaries into multiple CZ gates?
items.prior: Generic two-qubit unitaries required three CZ gates interleaved with single-qubit rotations in neutral-atom platforms.
items.limits: Numerical simulation assuming dispersive Rydberg dressing; dressing-state admixture in the computational manifold assumed < 10⁻³; optimization threshold 10⁻¹².
items.tools: Ashhab–Nori (AshN) control scheme · RF-dressed Förster resonance · GRAPE quantum optimal control · Rydberg state pair potentials
items.caption: Förster defect δ_F versus dressing frequency f_D, and interaction ratio J_z/J alongside Zeeman shift h₀ versus δ_F and atomic separation R, mapping out the required J_z/J ∈[-1, 0] range.
items.abstract: We propose a unified architecture for two-qubit gates in neutral-atom quantum processors which allows the implementation of the complete set of two-qubit gates. Our approach rests on a single resource that unlocks the entire gate set: an XXZ interaction with tunable anisotropy, combined only with single-qubit operations. We introduce a Rydberg-atom realization of the tunable XXZ interaction and combine it with optimally controlled global microwave pulses to implement the B, QFT, iSWAP, and √iSWAP gates, as well as a continuous gate family interpolating from CZ to iSWAP via the B gate. This work allows the implementation of any two-qubit gate natively in neutral-atom platforms, enabling flexible switching between instruction sets to reduce circuit depth and compilation overhead in quantum algorithm implementation.

items.title: The energetic cost of loading classical data in quantum computers
items.authors: Joao F. Doriguello, Alessandro Luongo, Harshit Verma
items.matched: Noise-Adaptive Compiler Mappings for Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum Computers
items.result: Querying a 12-qubit address bucket-brigade QRAM achieves fidelity 0.969 while consuming 3.51×10⁻⁴ J dynamic energy, averaging 4.38 W dynamic power with 64.4 W peak.
items.question: What is the physical dynamic energetic cost of loading classical data via QRAM architectures on superconducting quantum hardware?
items.limits: Theoretical and numerical optimization model assuming transmon superconducting gates; accounts for dynamic drive power, thermal photons, and attenuation profiles, excluding static cryostat cooling overhead.
items.tools: metric-noise-resource framework · bucket-brigade QRAM architecture · linear-depth multiplexer QRAM · superconducting gate decomposition schedule · multi-stage dilution refrigerator thermal model
items.abstract: Quantum algorithms for machine learning, chemistry, and cryptanalysis often assume coherent access to classical data at negligible physical cost. We instead treat data loading as a hardware process and quantify the dynamic energetic cost of a quantum random access memory (QRAM) query on a superconducting processor. Using the metric-noise-resource framework, we relate query fidelity and power to gate duration, relative two-qubit drive strength, and the distribution of attenuation across a multi-stage refrigerator, while accounting for thermal photons and gate errors. We analyze the linear-depth multiplexer and the noise-resilient bucket-brigade architectures, adapting the latter to a native superconducting gate set and refining its fidelity analysis using the fully decomposed gate schedule. For a representative bucket-brigade QRAM query with a 12-qubit address register we obtain a query fidelity of 0.969. The query consumes 3.51×10⁻⁴ J of dynamic energy, corresponding to an average dynamic power of 4.38 W and a peak of 64.4 W. Our optimization shows that, at fixed target fidelity, the operating point and attenuation profile can change the average power by a factor of two or more.

items.title: Cross-Platform Benchmarking of GHZ-State Generation in Quantum Processors via Cloud Services
items.authors: Sergio Hernández, Unai Aseguinolaza, David Aguirre, Marta Gili, Joseba Hernández, Guillermo Valverde, Uxue Ballarin Manso, Uxue Auzmendi, Iker Pastor, Pablo García Bringas, Ane Blázquez García, Rubén Peña, Mikel Sanz
items.result: Large superconducting quantum processors (107 to 156 qubits) support GHZ states passing genuine multipartite entanglement non-exclusion criteria on at most N^*=27 and N^*=24 qubits (<23% of register), whereas a 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes on its full register (N^*=12). Under a strict GME certification rule, only four of nine commercial processors succeed at any tested size.
items.question: How do commercial cloud-accessible quantum computing platforms across different hardware modalities compare when preparing genuine multipartite entangled GHZ states under standard end-user compilation?
items.limits: Default provider compilations without error mitigation; stabilizer sample size set by ε= δ= 0.10; evaluations limited to single runs or sparse binary-searched register sizes.
items.tools: QuSquare benchmark suite · Direct Fidelity Estimation (DFE) · remote cloud-access APIs (Amazon Braket, Qiskit Runtime) · superconducting and trapped-ion QPUs
items.caption: Comparison of largest passing GHZ size N^* against total physical qubits N_tot, alongside register utilization ratios and per-qubit GHZ error rates across nine processors.
items.abstract: Quantum computing has rapidly evolved into a diverse ecosystem of hardware platforms that differ in their underlying technologies and operational characteristics. Consequently, benchmarking has become essential for identifying the strengths of quantum processors, comparing their performance, and enabling informed decisions when selecting the most appropriate quantum computing platform for specific applications. In this work, we benchmark nine commercially accessible quantum processors from five vendors, spanning superconducting and trapped-ion technologies, using the multipartite entanglement benchmark from the QuSquare suite. All experiments were performed through remote cloud-access services, with the default compilation of each provider and without error mitigation, reflecting the performance experienced by end users. The benchmark estimates the fidelity of Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger (GHZ) states by direct fidelity estimation and searches for the largest GHZ state whose fidelity is compatible, within the statistical error, with the genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) threshold F=1/2. Our results reveal a substantial gap between the total number of physical qubits available on a processor and the size of the largest GHZ state passing the benchmark: the best superconducting processors reach N^*=27 and N^*=24 qubits, less than a quarter of their registers, whereas the 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes with its full register. We further show that median calibration data are poor predictors of the benchmark outcome, and that the reported sizes depend strongly on the statistical decision rule: requiring certified GME reduces the number of devices that succeed at any tested size from nine to four. These results provide a baseline for future cross-platform benchmarking of quantum processors.

items.abstract: We theoretically investigate an analog implementation of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) for the weighted maximum cut problem (MaxCut) problem. The protocol uses a three-dimensional array of individually trapped Rydberg atoms driven by globally addressed laser pulses, with site-dependent detunings applied near the Rydberg resonance. As benchmarks, we consider twenty randomly weighted 3-regular graphs with 12 vertices each. Problem weights are encoded directly in the interatomic interaction energies by choosing appropriate three-dimensional atom positions. We compare two parameter-optimization strategies: discretized quantum annealing and warm-start initialization using a graph neural network (GNN). The combined optimization strategy creates a portfolio that outperforms the Goemans-Williamson (GW) rounding almost in all instances in the noiseless case. We analyze the sampling statistics and the total pulse-time cost of both approaches. Finally, we emulate the performance of the optimized schedules on quantum trajectories using a realistic error model of the Aquila neutral-atom quantum processor.

items.abstract: Quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes can reduce the number of data qubits required per logical qubit, but their checks require long-range interactions on a planar device. We develop a singlet fabric for bivariate-bicycle codes on a silicon node network. Spin singlets are generated on shuttling lanes and distributed between nodes, where local operations consume them to measure non-local stabilizers. We construct two syndrome-extraction circuits, based on distributed GHZ states and ancilla teleportation, and evaluate them using hardware-constrained schedules and circuit-level memory simulations. We compare these circuits with CAbLECAR, which transports a mobile ancilla between the data qubits of each check. Teleportation can outperform CAbLECAR on its original layout when transport includes spin flips as well as dephasing. Placing the mobile ancilla on our node lattice, however, shortens the mean scheduled route for the [[144,12,12]] Gross code from 350 to 153 μm and lowers its logical error rate up to 50-fold in the sampled bit-flip regime. Direct transport then achieves a lower logical error rate than either singlet circuit at every sampled Gross-code point. With frequent transport bit flips, the GHZ circuit overtakes direct transport once two-qubit gate and readout errors fall below about 4-5×10⁻⁴, roughly half the value assumed here. Fixing the ancilla's data-visit order reveals a trade-off between shorter routes and the correlated errors produced by ancilla faults. Source heralding improves both singlet circuits, whereas phase purification helps the GHZ circuit only above a noise-dependent crossover and worsens teleportation throughout. These results show that the physical layout and interaction order can be as consequential as the choice of extraction circuit, and that cleaner entangled resources do not necessarily produce a more reliable logical memory.

items.title: Implementing rapid reset of superconducting qubits with on-chip dissipation
items.matched: Engineering cryogenic setups for 100-qubit scale superconducting circuit systems
items.result: Reset time constant median is 48.1 ns with 30 mK effective bath temperature. 400 ns reset pulse brings residual $|eangle$ population from 94.74% down to 0.67% across 20 transmon qubits.
items.question: Can on-chip resistive dissipation enable rapid, scalable transmon reset while isolating qubits from thermal noise of external circuitry?
items.limits: Demonstrated across 20 operational qubits measured in four nonadjacent groups on a 72-qubit chip to mitigate crosstalk. Measured median reset time 48.1 ns exceeds the 28.9 ns model prediction, likely due to dephasing and flux-pulse distortion.
items.tools: transmon qubits · dedicated λ/4 transmission-line resonators · thin-film PdAu resistive loads · flux-pulsed frequency tuning
items.caption: Single-shot readouts in the I-Q plane and cumulative distributions across 20 qubits comparing excited-state populations before and after a 400 ns reset pulse.
items.abstract: Rapid and high-fidelity qubit reset is essential for quantum state initialization and quantum error correction. Conventional reset protocols for superconducting qubits often rely on dissipative elements connected to external circuitry, exposing qubits to thermal noise from higher-temperature environments. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a scalable approach to qubit reset and leakage removal over multiple transmon qubits using dedicated dissipation units comprising resonators coupled to on-chip resistive loads. This architecture provides Purcell protection while isolating the qubits from warmer external circuitry. We achieve a median reset time constant of approximately 48 ns for the |g⟩-|e⟩ transition, with an effective bath temperature of 30 mK. A 400-ns reset pulse yields residual excited-state populations of 0.29% and 0.67% for qubits initialized in |g⟩ and |e⟩, respectively. We further demonstrate efficient leakage removal from the |f⟩ state, reducing its residual population to 0.51%. These results establish a simple, reproducible, and easy-to-integrate approach to dissipation engineering in superconducting quantum processors.

items.title: Cross-Platform Benchmarking of GHZ-State Generation in Quantum Processors via Cloud Services
items.result: Large superconducting quantum processors (107 to 156 qubits) support GHZ states passing genuine multipartite entanglement non-exclusion criteria on at most N^*=27 and N^*=24 qubits (<23% of register), whereas a 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes on its full register (N^*=12). Under a strict GME certification rule, only four of nine commercial processors succeed at any tested size.
items.question: How do commercial cloud-accessible quantum computing platforms across different hardware modalities compare when preparing genuine multipartite entangled GHZ states under standard end-user compilation?
items.limits: Default provider compilations without error mitigation; stabilizer sample size set by ε= δ= 0.10; evaluations limited to single runs or sparse binary-searched register sizes.
items.tools: QuSquare benchmark suite · Direct Fidelity Estimation (DFE) · remote cloud-access APIs (Amazon Braket, Qiskit Runtime) · superconducting and trapped-ion QPUs
items.caption: Comparison of largest passing GHZ size N^* against total physical qubits N_tot, alongside register utilization ratios and per-qubit GHZ error rates across nine processors.
items.abstract: Quantum computing has rapidly evolved into a diverse ecosystem of hardware platforms that differ in their underlying technologies and operational characteristics. Consequently, benchmarking has become essential for identifying the strengths of quantum processors, comparing their performance, and enabling informed decisions when selecting the most appropriate quantum computing platform for specific applications. In this work, we benchmark nine commercially accessible quantum processors from five vendors, spanning superconducting and trapped-ion technologies, using the multipartite entanglement benchmark from the QuSquare suite. All experiments were performed through remote cloud-access services, with the default compilation of each provider and without error mitigation, reflecting the performance experienced by end users. The benchmark estimates the fidelity of Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger (GHZ) states by direct fidelity estimation and searches for the largest GHZ state whose fidelity is compatible, within the statistical error, with the genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) threshold F=1/2. Our results reveal a substantial gap between the total number of physical qubits available on a processor and the size of the largest GHZ state passing the benchmark: the best superconducting processors reach N^*=27 and N^*=24 qubits, less than a quarter of their registers, whereas the 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes with its full register. We further show that median calibration data are poor predictors of the benchmark outcome, and that the reported sizes depend strongly on the statistical decision rule: requiring certified GME reduces the number of devices that succeed at any tested size from nine to four. These results provide a baseline for future cross-platform benchmarking of quantum processors.
